entities.name: Pioneer Kitten
entities.evidence: This advisory outlines activity by a specific group of Iranian cyber actors that has conducted a high volume of computer network intrusion attempts against U.S. organizations since 2017 and as recently as August 2024.

entities.name: xplfinder
entities.evidence: as of 2024, they have been operating under the moniker "xplfinder" in their channels.

entities.name: Iranian cyber actors
entities.evidence: a group of Iran-based cyber actors continues to exploit U.S. and foreign organizations.

entities.name: Danesh Novin Sahand
entities.evidence: The group uses the Iranian company name Danesh Novin Sahand (identification number 14007585836), likely as a cover IT entity for the group’s malicious cyber activities.

entities.name: CVE-2024-24919
entities.evidence: scanning IP addresses hosting Check Point Security Gateways, probing for devices potentially vulnerable to CVE-2024-24919.

entities.name: CVE-2024-3400
entities.evidence: scanning IP addresses hosting Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and GlobalProtect VPN devices. The actors were likely conducting reconnaissance and probing for devices vulnerable to CVE-2024-3400.

entities.name: CVE-2019-19781
entities.evidence: Historically, this group has exploited organizations by leveraging CVE-2019-19781 and CVE-2023-3519 related to Citrix Netscaler

entities.name: T1190

entities.name: T1505.003
entities.evidence: Capture login credentials using webshells on compromised Netscaler devices and append to file named netscaler.1 in the same directory as the webshell [T1505.003][T1056].

entities.name: T1056
entities.evidence: Capture login credentials using webshells on compromised Netscaler devices and append to file named netscaler.1 in the same directory as the webshell [T1505.003][T1056].

entities.name: T1133
entities.evidence: Create the directory /xui/common/images/ on targeted IP addresses [T1133].

entities.name: T1136.001
entities.evidence: Create accounts on victim networks; observed names include “sqladmin$,” “adfsservice,” “IIS_Admin,” “iis-admin,” and “John McCain” [T1136.001].

entities.name: T1098
entities.evidence: Request exemptions to the zero-trust application and security policies for tools they intend to deploy on a victim network [T1098].

entities.name: T1053
entities.evidence: Create malicious scheduled task SpaceAgentTaskMgrSHR in Windows/Spaceport/ task folder. This task uses a DLL side-loading technique against the signed Microsoft SysInternals executable contig.exe, which may be renamed to dllhost.ext, to load a payload from version.dll. This file has been observed being executed from the Windows Downloads directory [T1053].

entities.name: T1505
entities.evidence: For persistence and as detection and mitigation occurs, the actors create a daily Windows service task with random eight characters and attempt execution of a similarly named DLL contained in the C:\Windows\system32\drivers\ directory. For example, a service named “test” was observed attempting to load a file located at C:\WINDOWS\system32\drivers\test.sys [T1505].

entities.name: T1078.003
entities.evidence: Repurpose compromised credentials from exploiting networking devices, such as Citrix Netscaler, to log into other applications (i.e., Citrix XenDesktop) [T1078.003].

entities.name: T1078.002
entities.evidence: Repurpose administrative credentials of network administrators to log into domain controllers and other infrastructure on victim networks [T1078.002].

entities.name: T1562.001
entities.evidence: Use administrator credentials to disable antivirus and security software, and lower PowerShell policies to a less secure level [T1562.001][T1562.010].

entities.name: T1562.010
entities.evidence: Use administrator credentials to disable antivirus and security software, and lower PowerShell policies to a less secure level [T1562.001][T1562.010].

entities.name: T1562.001
entities.evidence: Attempt to enter security exemption tickets to the network security device or contractor to get the actor’s tools allowlisted [T1562.001].

entities.name: T1059.001
entities.evidence: Use a compromised administrator account to initiate a remote desktop session to another server on the network. In one instance, the FBI observed this technique being used to attempt to start Microsoft Windows PowerShell Integrated Scripted Environment (ISE) to run the command “Invoke-WebRequest” with a URI including files.catbox[.]moe. Catbox is a free, online file hosting site the actors use as a repository/hosting mechanism [T1059.001].

entities.name: T1012
entities.evidence: Export system registry hives and network firewall configurations on compromised servers [T1012].

entities.name: T1482
entities.evidence: Exfiltrate account usernames from the victim domain controller, as well as access configuration files and logs—presumably to gather network and user account information for use in further exploitation efforts [T1482].

entities.name: T1219
entities.evidence: Deployment of Meshcentral to connect with compromised servers for remote access [T1219].

entities.name: T1572
entities.evidence: Use the open source tunneling tool Ligolo (ligolo/ligolo-ng) [T1572].

entities.name: T1572
entities.evidence: Use NGROK (ngrok[.]io) deployment to create outbound connections to a random subdomain [T1572].

entities.name: T1657
entities.evidence: After infiltrating victim networks, the actors collaborate with ransomware affiliates (including NoEscape, Ransomhouse, and ALPHV [aka BlackCat]) in exchange for a percentage of the ransom payments by providing affiliates with access to victim networks, locking victim networks, and strategizing to extort victims [T1657].

entities.name: TA0010
entities.evidence: The actors also conduct what is assessed to be separate set of malicious activity—stealing sensitive data from victims [TA0010], likely in support of the GOI.

The FBI assesses a significant percentage of these threat actors’ operations against US organizations are intended to obtain and develop network access to then collaborate with ransomware affiliate actors to deploy ransomware.
The FBI assesses these actors do not disclose their Iran-based location to their ransomware affiliate contacts and are intentionally vague as to their nationality and origin.

This includes organizations across several sectors in the U.S. (including in the education, finance, healthcare, and defense sectors as well as local government entities) and other countries (including in Israel, Azerbaijan, and the United Arab Emirates).
